## Warm-Up: Sample Variability {.smaller}

According to 2022 data, 12.9% of college students in Michigan are enrolled in private institutions.

Suppose we take a random sample of 100 Michigan college students and compute the sample proportion enrolled in private institutions, $\hat p$.

**Turn and talk (60 sec):**

1. Will $\hat p$ be exactly 0.129? Why or why not?
2. If every student here took their own random sample of 100, what would the distribution of the $\hat p$ values look like (center and spread)?
3. What would change with samples of 500?

::: aside
Source: 2022 Michigan college enrollment data, as given in the class examples.
:::

::: notes
Goal: let them discover sampling variability before any formula. Expect: no, $\hat p$ varies from sample to sample; the distribution is centered near 0.129; spread around 0.03 for n = 100; narrower for n = 500 (about 0.015). Then go straight to StatKey to check their predictions.
:::

## StatKey Simulation {.smaller}

1. In StatKey, choose **Sampling Distribution for a Proportion**; set $p = 0.129$ and $n = 100$.
2. Generate 1000 samples. Record the **mean**, the **standard deviation** (this is the SE) and the **shape** of the simulated $\hat p$ values.
3. Change to $n = 500$ and repeat.

<table class="fillin">
<tr><th class="lab">Sample size</th><th style="width:9em">Shape</th><th>Mean</th><th>SE</th></tr>
<tr><td class="lab">\(n = 100\)</td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td class="lab">\(n = 500\)</td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
</table>

**Turn and talk (30 sec):** What do you notice about the SE when the sample size went from 100 to 500?

::: notes
Expected StatKey results (each simulation will differ a little): n = 100: mean about 0.129, SE about 0.034 (theory 0.0335), shape roughly normal with a slight right skew. n = 500: mean about 0.129, SE about 0.015 (theory 0.0150), shape very close to normal. A 5-fold increase in n cuts the SE by a factor of about $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$. Use this to motivate the formula on the next slide. Menu wording in StatKey may differ slightly from what is written here.
:::

## Standard Error for Sample Proportions


* For random samples of size $n$ from a population with proportion $p$, the **standard error of the sample proportion** $\hat p$ is

$$
SE=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}
$$


* The larger the sample size $n$, the smaller the SE.

::: notes
Have them check the formula against the StatKey values they just recorded: 0.0335 for n = 100 and 0.0150 for n = 500.
:::


## The Central Limit Theorem for Proportions

* If $n$ is sufficiently large,
$$
\hat p \sim N\left(p,\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\right)
$$

* A normal distribution is a good approximation as long as

  + $np\ge 10$ **and**

  + $n(1-p)\ge 10$


## Example 1: Michigan Students {.smaller}

According to 2022 data, 12.9% of college students in Michigan are enrolled in private institutions. For random samples of size $n$, describe the shape, mean, and standard error of the distribution of sample proportions for

<table class="fillin">
<tr><th class="lab"></th><th>\(np\)</th><th>\(n(1-p)\)</th><th style="width:9em">Shape</th><th>Mean</th><th>SE</th></tr>
<tr><td class="lab" style="white-space:nowrap"><span>a)</span> \(n = 100\)</td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td class="lab" style="white-space:nowrap"><span>b)</span> \(n = 500\)</td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr>
</table>

c\) What is the effect of the larger sample size on the shape, mean, and standard error?

::: {.ws .ed contenteditable="true"}
:::

::: notes
(a) np = 12.9 and n(1 - p) = 87.1, both at least 10, so approximately normal (n = 100 is the borderline case; mention the slight right skew they saw in StatKey). Mean 0.129. SE = sqrt(0.129 x 0.871 / 100) = 0.0335.

(b) np = 64.5 and n(1 - p) = 435.5, approximately normal, mean 0.129, SE = 0.0150.

(c) Shape: closer to normal. Mean: unchanged at 0.129 (center is p, no matter the n). SE: smaller by a factor of about $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.24$, so estimates from bigger samples are more precise.
:::

## Confidence Interval for a Single Proportion

A confidence interval for a population proportion $p$ can be computed using
$$
\hat p \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}
$$

if $n$ is large enough so that

* $n\hat p\ge 10$ and

* $n (1-\hat p)\ge 10$

## Example 2: Movie Goers {.smaller}

In a random sample of 1000 US adults in August 2022, 550 of them said they are more likely to wait and watch a new movie in the comfort of their own home.

a) Check the sample size conditions and find a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of movie goers who are more likely to watch a new movie from home. (Use $z^* = 1.96$.)

::: {.ws-l}
:::

b) Interpret the interval in context.

::: {.ws .ed contenteditable="true"}
:::

::: aside
Source: Morning Consult survey of US adults, August 2022 (reported by Statista).
:::

::: notes
$\hat p = 0.55$; conditions: 550 and 450 are both at least 10. SE = sqrt(0.55 x 0.45 / 1000) = 0.0157. ME = 1.96 x 0.0157 = 0.0308. 95% CI: 0.55 plus or minus 0.031, i.e. about (0.519, 0.581).

Interpretation: we are 95% confident that between about 51.9% and 58.1% of movie goers (US adults) are more likely to wait and watch a new movie at home.

If you are short on time, this example can be skipped or assigned: the coffee activity practices the same skills with the class's own data.
:::

## Coffee: Confidence Interval {.smaller}

Recall: use your $n$ and $\hat p$ from the previous slide.

5. Check the sample size conditions and construct a 95% confidence interval for the parameter defined in #4.

::: {.ws-l}
:::

Interpret the interval in context.

::: {.ws-l .ed contenteditable="true"}
:::

::: notes
$\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$. Check $n\hat p \ge 10$ and $n(1-\hat p) \ge 10$. If the class is small and few people drank coffee, the condition may fail; that is a teachable moment (then pool with the other section or use StatKey's bootstrap).

Interpretation template: we are 95% confident that between ___ and ___ of [population] drank coffee this morning. Remind them of the sampling caveat (the class is not a random sample).
:::

## Hypothesis Testing for a Single Proportion

To test $H_0:p=p_0$, we use the standardized test statistic
$$
z=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}
$$
where $\hat p$ is the proportion in a random sample of size $n$.

* Check sample size conditions:
  + $np_0\ge 10$
  + $n(1-p_0)\ge 10$

## Computing the P-value

* The appropriate $p$-value depends on the alternative hypothesis:


| Alternate Hypothesis 	|         $p$-value        	|
|:--------------------:	|:------------------------:	|
| $H_a: p>p_0$         	|        $P(Z\ge z)$       	|
| $H_a: p < p_0$       	|        $P(Z\le z)$       	|
| $H_a:p\neq p_0$      	| $2P(Z\ge z)$ if $z\ge 0$ 	|
| $H_a:p\neq p_0$      	|   $2P(Z\le z)$ if $z<0$  	|

If a student asks about the genetics: tongue rolling used to be presented as a simple dominant trait, but twin studies showed it is not that simple. That is fine to mention after the test, since the "75%" claim is only the hypothesis we are checking.

## Tongue Rolling: The Test {.smaller}

Tongue rolling has been said to be a dominant trait, in which case theoretically 75% of all people should be able to roll their tongues. Do our data provide evidence otherwise?

a) State the null and alternative hypotheses.

::: {.ws}
:::

b) Check the sample size conditions.

::: {.ws}
:::

::: notes
(a) $H_0: p = 0.75$ versus $H_a: p \ne 0.75$ (two-sided because the question asks for evidence "otherwise").

(b) Need $np_0 = 0.75n \ge 10$ (n at least 14) and $n(1-p_0) = 0.25n \ge 10$ (n at least **40**). Heads up: if the class has fewer than 40 students, the second condition fails. Options: pool with the other section or last term's survey data, or acknowledge the normal approximation is shaky and use StatKey's randomization test for a single proportion.
:::

## Tongue Test, Continued {.smaller}

Recall: the claim is that 75% of all people can roll their tongues.

c) Find the test statistic and the $p$-value.

::: {.ws-l}
:::

d) State your conclusion in context.

::: {.ws-l .ed contenteditable="true"}
:::

::: notes
(c) $z = (\hat p - 0.75)/\sqrt{0.75(0.25)/n}$; p-value is $2P(Z \ge |z|)$.

(d) Compare the p-value to a significance level (0.05): small p-value means the data provide evidence the proportion differs from 0.75; large p-value means no evidence against 75% (not proof that it is 75%). Also remind them of the sampling caveat.
:::

## Dice: Testing for Fairness {.smaller}

Let $p$ be the proportion of rolls (ignoring ties) in which the **white** die is greater than the red die.

a) If both dice are fair, what value should $p$ have, and why?

::: {.ws .ed contenteditable="true"}
:::

b) State the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the dice are fair.

::: {.ws}
:::

::: notes
(a) For two fair dice, P(white greater) = 15/36, P(red greater) = 15/36, P(tie) = 6/36. Ignoring ties leaves 15/30 = 0.5, so $p = 0.5$.

(b) $H_0: p = 0.5$ versus $H_a: p \ne 0.5$.

Do not reveal that the dice are rigged yet.
:::

## Dice: Pooled Class Results {.smaller}

Recall: $p$ is the proportion of non-tied rolls in which the WHITE die is greater.

<table class="fillin">
<tr><td class="lab">WHITE greater</td><td style="width:6em"></td><td class="lab">RED greater</td><td style="width:6em"></td><td class="lab">Total \(n\)</td><td style="width:6em"></td><td class="lab">\(\hat p\)</td><td style="width:6em"></td></tr>
</table>

c) Check the sample size conditions and find the test statistic and the $p$-value.

::: {.ws-l}
:::

d) State your conclusion in context.

::: {.ws-l .ed contenteditable="true"}
:::

::: notes
Pull the totals from the Forms responses (export to Excel and sum the two columns) and fill in the table live. Conditions: $np_0 = n(1-p_0) = 0.5n \ge 10$ needs n of at least 20, which pooled data easily meets. $z = (\hat p - 0.5)/\sqrt{0.5(0.5)/n}$; two-sided p-value $= 2P(Z \ge |z|)$.

If the p-value is small, the data provide strong evidence the dice are not fair; this is the moment to reveal the trick dice. Natural follow-up to ask: how lopsided are they? That is what a confidence interval for $p$ answers.
:::

## Sample Size for a Desired Margin of Error {.smaller}

To estimate a population proportion to within a desired margin of error, $\text{ME}$ with a given level of confidence, choose $n$ such that
$$
n=\left(\frac{z^*}{\text{ME}}\right)^2 \tilde p (1-\tilde p)
$$

where $\tilde p$ is either

* A guessed value for $p$ (if one is available) OR


* $\tilde p=0.5$ if no other guess is available

  +  Setting $\tilde p=0.5$ will ensure that $n$ is large enough no matter what $p$ turns out to be.

::: notes
Natural stopping point: if time is short, start next class here, with Example 3 and then move on to the next section.
:::

## Example 3: Sample Size {.smaller}

Recall (Example 2): $n = 1000$, $\hat p = 0.55$, 95% confidence ($z^* = 1.96$).

a) What is the margin of error for the confidence interval found in Example 2?

::: {.ws}
:::

b) What sample size is needed if we want a margin of error within ±2%? (Use the sample proportion from the original sample.)

::: {.ws}
:::

c) What sample size is needed if we want a margin of error within ±2%, and if we use the conservative estimate of $p = 0.5$?

::: {.ws}
:::

::: notes
(a) ME = 1.96 x sqrt(0.55 x 0.45 / 1000) = 0.0308 (about 3.1 percentage points); it is the "plus or minus" part of the interval.

(b) $n = (1.96/0.02)^2(0.55)(0.45) = 2376.99$, so n = 2377 (always round up).

(c) $n = (1.96/0.02)^2(0.5)(0.5) = 2401$.

Compare (b) and (c): the conservative estimate asks for slightly more people but guarantees the ME no matter what p turns out to be.
:::

## Wrapping Up {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
* The SE of $\hat p$ shrinks as $n$ grows, and $\hat p$ is approximately normal when $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$.
* A confidence interval for $p$ uses $\hat p$ in the SE: $\hat p \pm z^* \sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$.
* A test of $H_0: p = p_0$ uses $p_0$ in the SE, and the conditions are checked with $p_0$.
* The same data can be used to estimate $p$ (interval) or to check a claim about $p$ (test).
* Plan sample size from the margin of error you want, using $\tilde p = 0.5$ when you have no guess.
:::
